# Binary Jensen filters: a sharp relative bound and exact diamond products

This note gives two scoped results. First, an integral Jensen-graph filter supported on m integer height vectors has Helly number at most the sum of the Helly numbers of those height slices, hence at most m h(P). For one binary height coordinate the resulting factor 2 is sharp uniformly in dimension, even for globally affine heights. Second, independent copies of the ten-point diamond construction have EXACT unfiltered and filtered Helly numbers 8^r and 9^r, and exact coarse/fine simplex-source depths Gamma_s/2^r and Gamma_s/9^r.

The product calculation disproves compensation by the change in Gamma alone. The binary bound is not asserted for a coordinate taking arbitrarily many distinct integer heights. None of the results gives a sharp budget for general varying convex fibers.

## 1. A relative Helly bound from the actual integer height slices

Let P be a finite subset of a real vector space, and let g:P->R^r preserve every convex representation landing in P. Its full graph G(P) has the same Helly number as P: graph membership in the convex hull of a subset is equivalent to base membership by Jensen affinity, so all deletion-kernel tests agree.

For an integer vector a in Z^r put

    S_a={(p,g(p)):p in P, g(p)=a},
    A={a in Z^r:S_a is nonempty},
    T=union_(a in A) S_a.

Only finitely many slices are nonempty. We have

    h(T) <= sum_(a in A) h(S_a) <= |A| h(P).              (1)

Two elementary facts prove this. For a finite source S and a convex set C, h(S intersect C)<=h(S): append C to any family excluding S intersect C and apply the Helly property for S. For finitely many sources, h(union S_i)<=sum h(S_i), by choosing a subfamily excluding each S_i and taking their union. Each S_a is the intersection of G(P) with an affine height plane, giving (1).

Consequently, if every coordinate of the INTEGER height vectors occurring in T takes at most two values, then

    h(T)<=2^r h(P).                                      (2)

The sharper first inequality in (1) retains the actual height-slice geometry. Neither (1) nor (2) assumes that g is globally affine or that the filtered base set is lattice-convex in the old lattice.

There is a limited but valid source-depth consequence. If the actual source is the literal product conv(T) times one common s-dimensional convex body K, with its positive integer base set exactly T, then

    max depth >= Gamma_s/h(T)
       >= Gamma_s / sum_a h(S_a).                        (3)

Indeed the uniform finite base law on T has a point of depth at least 1/h(T). This follows directly from finite Helly: complements of base caps having mass strictly below 1/h(T) cannot exclude every T point, since at most h(T) such caps cannot cover its total mass. At the chosen base point put the ordinary centroid of K. Any ambient cap through that point contains centroids of at least a 1/h(T) fraction of the fibers. Each such fiber pays at least Gamma_s of its volume by ordinary continuous Grunbaum. Vertical caps pay at least 1/h(T). This proves (3) for the stated common-product source, without a general centroid selector assumption.

If P is lattice-convex in Z^k and g rational, conv(T) has exactly T as its integer points, as proved in the arithmetic note. Thus the literal product in (3) is an actual mixed source, after an intrinsic lattice reduction if its base graph has deficient affine rank. For binary heights, (2) and h(P)<=2^k give the actual rank-(k+r) target Gamma_s/2^(k+r) in this restricted product class. This is relative height-slice accounting, not an improvement of the general mixed Helly theorem.

## 2. The factor two is sharp, and lattice index is different from rank

For any m>=1 let

    P_m={0,+e_1,-e_1,...,+e_m,-e_m} subset Z^m.

It is the full integer set of the unit l1 ball, and

    h(P_m)=m+1.                                         (4)

The simplex {0,e_1,...,e_m} gives the lower bound: its convex hull contains no other P_m point and all its m+1 points are vertices. For the upper bound, consider any possible critical subset of size at least m+2. If it contains 0, its other points contain an opposite pair, so 0 lies in the convex hull of the others and the subset is not in convex position. If it does not contain 0, it contains at least TWO disjoint opposite pairs. Their common midpoint 0 remains in every deletion hull, preventing criticality. This is exactly the finite Helly-kernel criterion, and proves (4).

Now use the globally affine rational height

    g_m(p)=(1+sum_i p_i)/2.

At +e_i the height is 1, at -e_i it is 0, and at 0 it is 1/2. The integral graph consists of all 2m lifted crosspolytope vertices, and no other source points. It is in convex position, hence

    h(T_m)=2m,
    h(T_m)/h(P_m)=2m/(m+1) -> 2.                         (5)

Thus the constant 2 in the one-coordinate version of (2) cannot be decreased uniformly over dimension. The exact slice bound is attained: each of the height-zero and height-one slices is an (m-1)-simplex with m source vertices, so their Helly numbers sum to 2m.

This example also separates lattice INDEX from integer affine rank. The graph lies in

    2u-sum_i p_i=1.

Its affine integer lattice has rank m, not m+1. Projection onto p identifies it with the odd-parity coset {p in Z^m:sum_i p_i is odd}, an index-two coset of a rank-m lattice. Removing the fractional center raises h from m+1 to 2m while the saturated graph-lattice rank remains m. Therefore a proposed relative-h bound depending only on an increase of that rank, with no lattice-index data, is already false in this affine example. The ambient-coordinate statement (2) remains valid.

## 3. Exact Helly products of the ten-point gadget

Use the ten-point P'=W union {p_2}, height g, and nine-point integral graph T'=W_hat from `candidate a2bca99efffd5fb9`.

Besides h(P')=8 and h(T')=9, P' contains an EMPTY convex-position eight-subset

    U={p_0,p_1,p_2,p_4,p_5,p_7,p_8,p_10}.                (6)

The only omitted points are p_3 and p_6. On the supporting face y=0 the selected points are the triangle p_0,p_1,p_2. The omitted p_3 has z=2 and p_6 has x=2, whereas that triangle has x,z<=1. Thus neither omitted point belongs to conv(U). All selected W points retain their old exposures, and p_2 is an exposed vertex of the triangle (extended to the ambient hull by a sufficiently large negative y coefficient). Hence conv(U) intersect P'=U, with all eight points vertices. Since P' is lattice-convex, conv(U) has no other integer points either.

For r>=1 define

    P_r=(P')^r subset Z^(3r),
    g_r(p^(1),...,p^(r))=(g(p^(1)),...,g(p^(r))).

The map is Jensen-affine coordinatewise. Its integral graph is exactly

    T_r=(T')^r,

up to reordering coordinates. Since conv(U^r)=conv(U)^r, it contains exactly U^r as integer points and has all 8^r product vertices. This gives h(P_r)>=8^r; the lattice Helly bound in 3r coordinates gives the reverse inequality. All 9^r points of T_r are vertices of their product hull, so its finite Helly number equals its cardinality. Therefore

    h(P_r)=8^r,       h(T_r)=9^r.                        (7)

The arithmetic increase is exactly (9/8)^r, with r separate added integer-coordinate tests.

The sharper bound in (1) is exact here. In a single gadget the integral height-zero slice consists of seven W points and the height-one slice of two, all in convex position. A binary height vector with j ones therefore has 2^j 7^(r-j) product vertices. Summing the exact slice Helly numbers gives

    sum_(a in {0,1}^r) h(S_a)=(7+2)^r=9^r=h(T_r).        (8)

Thus the needed height-slice budget can genuinely exceed the unfiltered Helly budget; the slice terms cannot in general be collapsed back to h(P_r).

## 4. Exact product source depths, all ambient cap directions

Fix an s-simplex K, s>=1, of volume V and centroid c, and set

    C_(r,s)=conv(T_r) times K.

This is full-dimensional in R^(4r+s), and is the convex hull of its actual fine mixed set. Its fine integer base set is T_r, consisting of 9^r positive fibers equal to K. Dropping the r height-integrality conditions gives the coarse source with base set P_r, consisting of 10^r equal K fibers located at the vector height g_r(p). Every coarse full (r+s)-dimensional fiber volume is zero.

The exact fine maximum follows from own-simplex centroids and a finite isolating cap cover, as before:

    max fine depth = Gamma_s/9^r.                        (9)

For clarity the upper cover can use the sum of the single-coordinate integer exposure penalties. It vanishes only at its target T_r point, is at least one at every other fine point, and a tilt of two isolates every canonical simplex cap. The lower bound uses the one own fiber. No product-depth inference is needed.

The exact coarse maximum is

    max coarse depth = Gamma_s/2^r.                      (10)

For its lower bound choose the base (p_2,...,p_2), the height vector (1/2,...,1/2), and the continuous point c. The 5^r bases in the product of the five-point diamonds are centrally symmetric about this graph base. Restricted to these fibers, the source is one uniform K plus an independent symmetric finite additive displacement in the cap's scalar normal direction. The proved paired-centroid-tail theorem, equivalently its symmetric-noise corollary in `candidate 732b11a769399016`, gives cap mass at least Gamma_s 5^r V. If the continuous x-normal is zero, closed symmetry gives at least half this subsource, which is enough because Gamma_s<=1/2. Dividing by the full coarse mass 10^r V proves the lower bound in (10).

Here is a matching upper bound at EVERY coarse point. For a single target index i in P' define the affine nonnegative penalty on P'

    a_2(p)=y(p),
    a_i(p)=n_i dot(p_i-p),          i in W,

where n_i is the old exposing normal. The first penalty vanishes exactly on the five-point diamond; the others vanish only at p_i, including strict positivity at p_2. All nonzero penalty values on P' are integers at least one.

For a target (i_1,...,i_r), add these r penalties. If k of its coordinates equal 2, the sum vanishes at exactly 5^k coarse bases and is at least one elsewhere. The caps

    lambda_l(x)-1/(s+1)-2 sum_j a_(i_j)(p^(j))>=0

therefore each have mass Gamma_s 5^k V, and the s+1 such caps cover the target fiber. Since k<=r, every coarse point has depth at most Gamma_s 5^r/10^r, proving (10). This explicitly handles every coarse base and every possible continuous point; no eligibility assertion is left implicit.

Combining (9)--(10),

    max fine depth / max coarse depth = (2/9)^r.          (11)

The fine retained mass is a fraction (9/10)^r of the coarse intrinsic mass. The center-admissibility change is therefore essential, beyond merely comparing total masses.

## 5. Gamma cannot absorb the arithmetic loss

The strict convexity

    (log Gamma_t)''=1/[t(t+1)^2]>0,  t>0,

implies Gamma_(j+1)/Gamma_j>=8/9 for every integer j>=1, strictly for j>=2. Multiplying these r ratios gives

    Gamma_(s+r)/Gamma_s >= (8/9)^r,

with equality only for s=r=1. Hence

    Gamma_s/9^r <= Gamma_(s+r)/8^r,                       (12)

strictly for every other pair s,r>=1. The right-hand side is the naive coarse-rank-3r target using the larger continuous ambient dimension s+r. The actual fine rank is 4r and its OC target Gamma_s/16^r remains strictly below (9).

For fixed s and r tending to infinity, the ratio of the left side of (12) to the right side is

    (8/9)^r Gamma_s/Gamma_(s+r) -> 0.

Thus even a fixed positive multiplicative fraction of that naive coarse target cannot hold for all these product sources. This is a certified obstruction to compensation using only Gamma's dimension change. It does not determine an optimal general tradeoff for arbitrary rational characters and arbitrary convex fibers.

The verifier `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_binary_filter_and_diamond_products.py` checks the empty eight-subset, exact crosspolytope kernel classification in finite dimensions, product counts and slice sums, penalties and depth ratios, and Gamma identities. The proofs above establish the statements for all r,s,m in their stated ranges.

This is a pending mathematical submission, not an accepted fact. Its definitions, scoped assertions, calculations, and limitations are given in the proposed argument below. A reference to another pending candidate supplies context only; it is not an accepted premise.

# Binary Jensen filters: a sharp relative bound and exact diamond products

**Helly accounting for binary Jensen filters**

A Jensen graph preserves the finite Helly number of its base set. Intersecting with a convex set does not increase it, and the Helly number of a finite union is at most the sum of the constituent Helly numbers. Hence, for a Jensen height map with r integer-valued coordinates such that each coordinate takes at most two values on the surviving set, the filtered graph has Helly number at most 2^r h(P). This is a bound for that specified two-value filter, not for arbitrary binary predicates.

Scope limits: This is a finite-source bound with the actual source Helly number. It does not supply the sharp geometric Gamma factor or an invariant retention theorem.
